=== Kennedy-Burrow Support Letter.pdf ===
     PUBLIC COMMENT IN SUPPORT OF THE KENNEDY–BURROW REQUEST FOR AN
     INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION AND FORENSIC AUDIT

     September 22, 2026

     PUC Docket Nos. 59029, 59182, 59315, 59336 and 59475

     Dear Governor Abbott, Chairman Gleeson and Commissioners:

     I support Kevin Kennedy and John Burrow’s request for an independent technical
     investigation and forensic audit of ERCOT’s 2024 Permian Basin Reliability Plan
     modeling. Their request appears in Docket 59475, Item 6571, and in a revised letter and
     memorandum addressed to Governor Abbott led in Docket 59336, Item 2745.

     I am an intervenor in the Howard–Solstice proceeding, Docket 59336, and a landowner
     whose family ranch is crossed by the approved route. I submit this public comment
     across all ve related dockets because the questions raised concern the shared
     planning foundation used to justify these projects.

     My central concern is straightforward: the Commission is barreling through
     approvals without rst requiring documented answers to important questions
     about need, cost, alternatives and conditions on the ground.

     Those answers should inform the decisions before they are made.

     The modeling deserves independent scrutiny.

     Kennedy and Burrow identify differences between ERCOT’s Permian Basin Reliability
     Plan and its contemporaneous Regional Transmission Plan, including assumptions
     about the location and timing of future electricity demand and generation. They ask
     whether those differences were appropriate, whether they affected the results, and
     whether the modeling established the need for each of the three 765-kV import paths.

     I am not claiming that differences between planning models, by themselves, prove
     misconduct or invalidate a project. Different studies may legitimately serve different
     purposes. But that makes a clear reconciliation essential when their conclusions are
     used to justify billions of dollars in infrastructure and permanent burdens on private
     property.

     The public deserves to know whether subsequent studies independently tested the
     need for these facilities or incorporated them into the starting assumptions. We also
     deserve to know whether each import path remains justi ed when demand, generation
     and network assumptions are reconciled.

     Demonstrating that a proposed transmission system can function is not the same as
     explaining why that particular system is necessary, at that capacity, on that timetable,
     and at that cost.

      A $452 Million Discrepancy Deserves an Explanation

     Another example reinforces the need to verify the numbers being presented in support
     of 765-kV development. Page 13 of the Siemens PTI study, led in Project No. 55718,
     Item 107, lists projected 2039 production costs of $16,471 million for the 345-kV option
     and $15,982 million for the 765-kV option, but reports a difference of $941 million. The
     displayed gures yield a difference of $489 million—a $452 million discrepancy. This
     may be a presentation or transcription error; it does not, by itself, establish a defect in
     the underlying model. But it warrants correction and an explanation of whether the
     discrepancy affects any subsequent analysis or claimed bene ts. An independent
     review should reconcile the published gures with the underlying calculations.




     Governor Abbott, apply the same scrutiny to the infrastructure as to the demand.

     Your data-center audit initiative recognizes the importance of verifying proposed
     demand before making consequential decisions. Kennedy and Burrow ask you to bring
     comparable scrutiny to the transmission modeling.

     I support that request.

     The extent to which audited data-center demand overlaps with the forecasts used in the
     Permian plan should be identi ed and explained. Where veri ed information materially
     changes the underlying assumptions, the state should require an explanation of what
     changes—and what does not—in the justi cation for the transmission projects.

           Landowners and ratepayers should not be expected to accept uncertainty in the
          underlying information while the consequences for their property and nances become
          increasingly permanent.

          Howard–Solstice provides a concrete example of the same problem.

          On September 18, I led a comment concerning the Armadillo Uvalde rock quarry:
          Docket 59336, Item 2743.

          That ling compares September 2025 and September 2026 satellite imagery with the
          applicants’ link map. The imagery shows substantial excavation at the quarry, and the
          approved alignment of Link 81A appears to run directly through it. The September 2,
          2026 image predates the Commission’s September 11 route-selection vote.

          As documented in my ling, Chairman Gleeson described the modi cation as an
          “elegant change,” and Commissioner Jackson called it “an example, quite frankly, of the
          process working.”

          An “elegant change” on a map deserves a less elegant question: Did anyone check
          whether it runs through an operating rock quarry?

          Immediately before the vote, AEP Texas’s Stephanie G. Houle assured the Commission
          that all routes were feasible from an engineering standpoint. My ling asks whether the
          quarry had been identi ed and evaluated when that assurance was given—and where
          the supporting analysis can be found.

          I have since been told that this quarry uses blasting. I have not independently veri ed
          that information, and I am not presenting it as an established fact. I am asking the
          Commission and applicants to verify it directly with the operator and determine whether
          blasting occurs, where it occurs, and what implications it may have for the proposed
          crossing.

          I am not asserting that a transmission line cannot cross a quarry. I am asking whether
          the Commission understood the quarry’s current operations, potential expansion,
          engineering constraints and associated costs before selecting the route.

          Were special structures, different tower locations, operational restrictions or route
          adjustments anticipated? Were those costs included in the route comparison? Who
          would bear any additional expense?

          General assurances that every link is viable do not answer those site-speci c questions.

          The quarry does not prove a modeling defect. It illustrates why veri cation must
          come rst.

          The quarry and the ERCOT modeling raise different technical issues, but they share a
          basic decision-making concern: are the underlying facts suf ciently current, accurate
          and complete to support the decision being made?

                     At the system level, that means verifying the assumptions used to establish need.

                    At the property level, it means identifying and evaluating material conditions along the
                    selected route.

                    Landowners should not have to discover those conditions after approval and then hope
                    they can be accommodated without additional expense, restrictions or impacts on
                    neighboring properties.

                    Nor should we have to accept that an independent examination of need can wait until
                    construction and nancial commitments make meaningful reconsideration increasingly
                    dif cult.

                    I respectfully request the following action:

                    1. Governor Abbott and the Commission should act on the Kennedy–Burrow request
                       by initiating an independent technical investigation and forensic audit of the Permian
                       Basin modeling.
                    2. The review should reconcile material differences in demand, generation, timing and
                       network assumptions; independently reproduce the relevant results; and evaluate
                       the justi cation for each of the three import paths.
                    3. The state should use the lawful authority available to pause further approvals and
                       implementation of the affected projects while that review is completed, with
                       particular attention to preventing irreversible land disturbance.
                    4. The ndings should be made public to the fullest extent permitted, with a meaningful
                       opportunity for scrutiny and legislative consideration.
                    5. In Howard–Solstice, the Commission should require a documented response to the
                       quarry questions raised in Item 2743, including veri cation of the reported blasting
                       and an explanation of any engineering, routing, operational and cost implications
                       before construction proceeds at that location.

                    These requests seek answers, accountability and informed decisions.

                    If the models withstand independent scrutiny, the state can explain that conclusion with
                    greater con dence. If they do not, Texans deserve to know while there is still an
                    opportunity to change course.

                    The Commission should be requiring answers before approval—not leaving landowners
                    to uncover the questions afterward.

                    Respectfully submitted,

                    Scott J Brown
                    Landowner and Intervenor, PUC Docket 59336
                    Submitted as public comment in PUC Docket Nos. 59029, 59182, 59315, 59336 and
                    59475
